lessons.title: Memorisation, Recitation and Translation (Nazira and Hifz)
lessons.notes_html:
Nazira Recitation (Reading by Looking)

This lesson is a memorisation and recitation lesson. For Nazira (reading the Quran by looking at it), the Surahs of the thirtieth Juz are prescribed:

  • Surah Al-Fil, Surah Quraysh, Surah Al-Ma'un, Surah Al-Kauthar, Surah Al-Kafirun, Surah An-Nasr, Surah Al-Lahab, Surah Al-Ikhlas, Surah Al-Falaq and Surah An-Naas.
  • Along with these, the first five verses and the last two verses of Surah Al-Baqarah and the last three verses of Surah Al-Hashr are also read by looking.

Hifz (Memorisation)

  • For memorisation: Ayat-ul-Kursi from Surah Al-Baqarah, Surah Al-Falaq and Surah An-Naas.
  • Besides these, Surah Al-Mulk is taught to the students by heart, and the first sixteen (16) verses of Surah Ar-Rahman are also given for memorisation.

Ayat-ul-Kursi: اللَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ ۚ لَا تَأْخُذُهُ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ ۚ لَّهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ ۗ مَن ذَا الَّذِي يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِ ۚ يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ ۖ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَيْءٍ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِ إِلَّا بِمَا شَاءَ ۚ وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ ۖ وَلَا يَئَودُهُ حِفْظُهُمَا ۚ وَهُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْعَظِيمُ

Surah Al-Falaq: قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ ۝ مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ ۝ وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ ۝ وَمِن شَرِّ النَّفَّاثَاتِ فِي الْعُقَدِ ۝ وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ

Surah An-Naas: قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ النَّاسِ ۝ مَلِكِ النَّاسِ ۝ إِلَٰهِ النَّاسِ ۝ مِن شَرِّ الْوَسْوَاسِ الْخَنَّاسِ ۝ الَّذِي يُوَسْوِسُ فِي صُدُورِ النَّاسِ ۝ مِنَ الْجِنَّةِ وَالنَّاسِ

Memorisation and Translation

Surah Al-Fatiha: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ ۝ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ ۝ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ ۝ مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ ۝ إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ ۝ اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ ۝ صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ

Its translation is: All praises are for Allah, the Lord of all the worlds. The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Master of the Day of Judgement. You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Guide us on the straight path — the path of those whom You have blessed, not of those who earned Your anger, nor of those who went astray.

The translation of Tashahhud (At-Tahiyyat) is: All verbal, physical and monetary worships are for Allah. O Prophet! Peace be upon you and the mercy and blessings of Allah. Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad (PBUH) is His servant and Messenger.

The translation of Durood-e-Ibrahimi is: O Allah! Bestow Your mercy upon Muhammad (PBUH) and his progeny, as You bestowed mercy upon Hazrat Ibrahim (A.S.) and his progeny; indeed You are Praiseworthy and Glorious. O Allah! Bestow Your blessings upon Muhammad (PBUH) and his progeny, as You bestowed blessings upon Hazrat Ibrahim (A.S.) and his progeny; indeed You are Praiseworthy and Glorious.

Supplications (Duas) to Memorise

  • The dua before sleeping, the dua after waking up, the dua for leaving the home, the dua for entering the home, and a dua asking forgiveness for oneself and for all Muslims (Rabbana zalamna...). These duas should be memorised and recited daily.
  • The translation of the dua before sleeping is: "O Allah! In Your name I die (sleep) and I live (awake)." This dua teaches us that sleep is also in Allah's power and waking up is also by His grace, so we should take Allah's name before sleeping.

Key Points

  • Nazira Surahs are from the thirtieth Juz, plus parts of Surah Al-Baqarah and Surah Al-Hashr.
  • Hifz includes Ayat-ul-Kursi, Surah Al-Falaq, Surah An-Naas, Surah Al-Mulk and the first 16 verses of Surah Ar-Rahman.
  • The translations of Surah Al-Fatiha, Tashahhud and Durood-e-Ibrahimi are learnt by heart.

lessons.title: The World is a Cultivating Field for the Hereafter
lessons.notes_html:
The World — a Field of the Hereafter

Just as a farmer reaps whatever he sows in his field, a person will receive the reward of whatever deeds he does in this world, in the Hereafter. Therefore we should sow the seeds of good deeds in this world so that we may harvest the crop of Paradise in the Hereafter.

  • This worldly life is given to us as a trial and a test, to see who performs good deeds and who does evil. The real purpose of life is the worship and obedience of Allah.
  • Success and happiness in the Hereafter are achieved by believing in Allah, obeying the Nabi Karim (PBUH) and performing good deeds — offering Namaz, keeping fasts, paying Zakat and staying away from sins.

The Day of Judgement

  • When Hazrat Israfil (A.S.) blows the trumpet for the first time, by the order of Allah, the whole world will be destroyed and all living beings will die. After it, the trumpet will be blown a second time and all human beings will come back to life.
  • Kiraman Katibeen are the two honourable angels appointed with every human being. Their duty is to keep writing down all the good and bad deeds of the person in his record of deeds.
  • On the Day of Judgement every person will be given his record of deeds: the righteous will receive it in their right hand, while the wicked will receive it in their left hand or from behind their back. Then the deeds will be weighed; whoever's good deeds are heavy will enter Paradise, and whoever's sins are heavy will go to Hell.

Key Points

  • Belief in the Hereafter is a basic tenet of Islam, and Paradise is a place full of blessings.
  • The life of this world is not forever — it is a field in which we sow deeds for the Hereafter.

lessons.title: Obedience of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) and its Importance
lessons.notes_html:
What is Ita'at-e-Rasool?

Obedience of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) means accepting every command of his and acting upon everything he said. Whoever obeys the Nabi Karim (PBUH) from the heart and spends his life according to his way is his true obedient follower. The word "Ita'at" is a word of the Arabic language, which means obedience — to obey and follow.

  • Verses for the chart on obedience: "O believers! Obey Allah and obey the Rasool." and "Whoever obeys the Rasool has indeed obeyed Allah." Hadith: "Whoever obeys me will enter Paradise."
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) is a role model for us, and Allah revealed the Holy Quran upon him.

Importance of Obedience

  • Allah Almighty has commanded obedience to the Nabi Karim (PBUH) again and again in the Holy Quran and has declared obedience to him as obedience to Allah Himself.
  • Without obeying the Nabi Karim (PBUH), our faith does not become complete; to decide and act according to his decision is an essential condition of faith.
  • Allah's pleasure is only in following the way of the Nabi Karim (PBUH), and success in this world and the Hereafter is gained only through his obedience, while disobeying him leads to going astray and failure.

The Companions and Obedience

The Companions (R.A.) were unmatched in obeying the Nabi Karim (PBUH). They followed his footsteps in every matter, accepted his every command without delay and gave preference to his liking over their own. Whether it was war or peace, happiness or hardship, they kept obeying him in every condition.

Key Points

  • For success in both the worlds, obedience to Allah and His Rasool (PBUH) and following his way (Sunnah) is essential.
  • One benefit of obedience to the Rasool is the completion of faith.

lessons.title: The Importance of the Sunnah of the Nabi Karim (PBUH)
lessons.notes_html:
What is Sunnah?

The Sunnah of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) means his way, his sayings and his actions. Whatever the Nabi Karim (PBUH) said, whatever he did and whatever he permitted in his life is all his Sunnah, and it is necessary for Muslims to act upon it. Whatever he ordered the Muslims, he himself acted upon it first and showed it.

  • Ayat: لَقَدْ كَانَ لَكُمْ فِي رَسُولِ اللَّهِ أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ — "Indeed, in the Rasool of Allah (PBUH) there is an excellent model for you." Allah has declared the life of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) to be the best pattern of action (Uswa-e-Hasana) for all people.
  • Ayat: وَمَا آتَاكُمُ الرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَانْتَهُوا — "And whatever the Rasool gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it."
  • Allah Almighty has made the personality of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) comprehensive and perfect for every human being.

Sunnah Explains the Worships

  • Namaz: the detailed method of offering Namaz (the number of Rakats, the manner and the details of timings) is not fully described in the Quran. The Nabi Karim (PBUH) taught the complete method through his Sunnah and said: "Offer Namaz as you see me offering it." Without the Sunnah, Namaz cannot be offered correctly.
  • Hajj: about its method the Nabi Karim (PBUH) said: "Learn the rites (methods) of Hajj from me." The details of Hajj are brief in the Quran and its practical form becomes clear through the Sunnah.
  • For explanation of the rulings and problems related to Saum (fasting, obligatory in Ramadan) too, we need to look into the Sunnah of the Nabi Karim (PBUH).

Key Points

  • Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) is the last Rasool of Allah, and his life is the best practical example for every Muslim.
  • The way of success is to follow the Holy Quran and the Sunnah — not to forget them.

lessons.title: Introduction and Social Importance of Friday and Eids
lessons.notes_html:
Friday Namaz

Friday has been declared the best day of the week. Friday Namaz is offered in congregation every Friday at the time of Zuhr, and it is obligatory upon every adult Muslim male. It has two obligatory Rakats, offered after the Khutbah (sermon), and it cannot be missed without a genuine and legitimate (Shar'i) excuse.

  • Etiquettes of Friday: taking a bath (Ghusl), wearing clean and good clothes, applying fragrance, reaching the masjid early, listening to the Khutbah silently and avoiding talking during it; reciting Durood abundantly and making dua are also among its etiquettes.
  • Objectives of congregational Namaz: unity and brotherhood are created among Muslims, everyone worships Allah standing equal in one row, people learn about each other's conditions, and an opportunity arises to help the weak and the poor. Through it the masjid remains inhabited and religious teaching spreads.
  • On Friday, after the Adhan, the Imam delivers the Khutbah, which everyone listens to silently; then the two obligatory Rakats are offered in congregation, and after the Namaz people meet one another and ask about each other's well-being.

The Two Eids

  • Allah has given Muslims two days in a year to celebrate happiness and Eid: Eid-ul-Fitr on 1st Shawwal and Eid-ul-Adha on 10th Dhu Al-Hijjah.
  • Eid-ul-Adha is celebrated in the remembrance of Hazrat Ibrahim's (A.S.) great sacrifice; halal animals are sacrificed on it after the Namaz, and the meat is distributed among the poor.
  • On Eid-ul-Fitr, the poor are included in the happiness by giving Fitrana — we should assist our needy brothers by helping them financially and sharing our happiness with them.
  • Manners of Eid Namaz: taking a bath and wearing clean or new clothes, applying fragrance, eating something sweet before the Namaz on Eid-ul-Fitr, going to the Eidgah by one route and returning by another, reciting Takbeers on the way, and saying "Eid Mubarak" to one another after the Namaz.
  • Social significance of Eids: all Muslims gather together, love and brotherhood increase, people forgive each other and end enmities, and feelings of equality and caring for one another are created in society.

Key Points

  • Friday Namaz: Zuhr time, in congregation, two Rakats after the Khutbah.
  • Eid-ul-Fitr — 1st Shawwal; Eid-ul-Adha — 10th Dhu Al-Hijjah.

lessons.title: Introduction of Saum (Fasting) and its Significance
lessons.notes_html:
What is Saum?

Saum is an Arabic word which literally means "to stop / to prevent". In Shariah, Saum means abstaining from eating, drinking and every bad deed from dawn (Subh-e-Sadiq) till sunset, with the intention of worshipping Allah. Fasting is obligatory upon every adult Muslim in Ramadan-ul-Mubarak, and it is one of the five pillars of Islam.

  • Ayat: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ — "O believers! Fasting has been made obligatory upon you, as it was made obligatory upon those before you, so that you may become pious." Saum is the worship which was also made compulsory for the previous nations.
  • The Holy Quran was revealed in the month of Ramadan, and in Ramadan the majority of Muslims frequently go to the masjids.

Virtues of Saum

  • Allah Almighty says that the fast is for Me and I Myself will give its reward.
  • All the previous sins of the fasting person are forgiven.
  • In Paradise there is a special gate called "Rayyan" through which only the fasting people will enter, and the fast will intercede for the fasting person on the Day of Judgement.

Benefits and Social Significance

  • Saum improves health and saves a person from many diseases; control over the self (nafs) is gained and the habit of patience is formed.
  • Fasting keeps a person away from sins and bad deeds and makes him adopt piety (Taqwa); nearness to Allah is achieved.
  • Saum creates an emotion of compassion for others: the fasting person himself feels hunger and thirst, so he feels for the poor and the hungry. In Ramadan people give more charity and care for one another, which increases love, brotherhood and equality in society.

Key Points

  • Saum = abstaining from food, drink and bad deeds from dawn till sunset for Allah's pleasure.
  • Its special gate in Paradise is Rayyan; its reward is given by Allah Himself.

lessons.title: Muwakhat (Brotherhood)
lessons.notes_html:
What is Muwakhat?

Muwakhat is a word of the Arabic language which means brotherhood. The bond of brotherhood which the Nabi Karim (PBUH) established in Madinah between the Muhajireen of Makkah and the Ansar of Madinah is called Muwakhat-e-Madinah. In Islamic history this relation became famous with this very name.

  • Muhajireen are those Muslims who, fed up with the cruelties and persecution of the pagans (disbelievers) of Makkah, left their homes and wealth and migrated to Madinah for the sake of Allah and His Rasool. Their occupation was trade.
  • Ansar means the helpers — those Muslims of Madinah who helped the Muhajireen, gave them space in their homes and shared their wealth with them. Allah Almighty gave them the title of Ansar. Their occupation was agriculture.
  • The Muhajireen had self-respect: they accepted help but preferred to earn by hard work.

The Method of Muwakhat

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) made each Muhajir the brother of one Ansari. Under this bond, the Ansar shared their wealth, homes and land with the Muhajireen, and the housing, employment and needs of the Muhajireen were fulfilled. In this way both became partners in each other's joys and sorrows, and a strong Islamic society was established in Madinah.

The Sacrifices of the Ansar

  • The Ansar shared their homes, gardens and lands with the Muhajireen, offered to give half of their wealth, and kept the Muhajireen like their own families. Through these sacrifices, the economic problems of the Muhajireen ended.
  • Hazrat Saad bin Rabi' (R.A.) offered half of his wealth and his house to his Muhajir brother Hazrat Abdul Rehman bin Auf (R.A.), but Abdul Rehman thanked him and said: "Just show me the way to the market", and he became prosperous through hard work. This incident teaches brotherhood, sacrifice and self-respect.

Key Points

  • Muwakhat = the brotherhood between Muhajireen and Ansar established by the Nabi Karim (PBUH) in Madinah.
  • Due to Muwakhat-e-Madinah, an Islamic society and brotherhood were established in Madinah.

lessons.title: Construction of Masjid-e-Nabawi
lessons.notes_html:
The First Order in Madinah

After arriving in Madinah, the first order given by the Nabi Karim (PBUH) was to build a Masjid. He selected the place where his camel had sat; the Nabi Karim (PBUH) entered Madinah riding a camel named Qaswa. That land belonged to two orphan brothers, Sahal and Suhail. Its price was paid and the construction of Masjid-e-Nabawi was started; the Nabi Karim (PBUH) himself took part in the work along with the Companions, and every Companion of Madinah wanted to be his host. The building of the Masjid was built with mud bricks, its length was one hundred hands, it had three doors, and at that time two rooms were constructed for the wives (Mothers of the Faithful) of the Nabi Karim (PBUH).

  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) stayed for some time at the house of Hazrat Abu Ayyub Ansari (R.A.), near the plot of the Masjid.

Virtues of Masjid-e-Nabawi

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) said that the reward of offering one Namaz in my this Masjid is more than offering a thousand Namaz in other Masjids, except Masjid-e-Haram (the Ka'bah). Therefore, offering Namaz in Masjid-e-Nabawi is a deed of great virtue and reward.

Suffah and Ashab-e-Suffah

  • A platform was built on the northern side of Masjid-e-Nabawi, which was called "Suffah".
  • The poor and needy Companions who lived there and gained knowledge from the Nabi Karim (PBUH) were called "Ashab-e-Suffah" (the Companions of the Platform). They remained busy day and night in worship and in gaining knowledge.

Social Significance

Masjid-e-Nabawi was the centre of the Muslims: along with Namaz, the decisions and consultations of the state were made there, delegations and guests stayed there, and the Ashab-e-Suffah gained education there and spread out to preach Islam. In this way, Masjid-e-Nabawi was a place of worship as well as a school, a court and a social centre.

Key Points

  • Land of the Masjid: the orphans Sahal and Suhail; its price was paid before building.
  • One Namaz in Masjid-e-Nabawi = more reward than a thousand Namaz elsewhere, except Masjid-e-Haram.

lessons.title: Charter of Madinah (Mithaq-e-Madinah)
lessons.notes_html:
What is the Charter of Madinah?

"Mithaq" is an Arabic word which means a charter, treaty, agreement or covenant. The Charter of Madinah (Mithaq-e-Madinah) is the agreement which the Nabi Karim (PBUH) concluded between the Muslims, the Jews and other tribes of Madinah to establish peace in the city and to make the new state strong and stable. This charter consisted of 54 articles, and it was the first written agreement, which laid the foundation of the Islamic state.

  • Three Jewish tribes were settled in Madinah: Banu Qainqa, Banu Nadhir and Banu Qurayzah.
  • The two Ansar tribes living in Madinah were Banu Aws and Banu Khazraj.

Important Articles

  • All the tribes will live in peace and harmony and will participate in establishing peace.
  • In case of an attack by an external enemy on Madinah, all will fight the enemy together and collectively bear the costs of the war; all parties will defend Madinah together.
  • All parties will recognise Madinah as "Haram" (a place of honour and peace) and will not cause any unrest in it.
  • Each party will have freedom of religion, and there will be no interference in the religious affairs of any other party.
  • The oppressed will be helped, and every party will solve its internal conflicts independently.
  • No party will give shelter to the Quraysh of Makkah.
  • In case of a disagreement, the decision of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) will be binding and accepted by all.

Benefits of the Charter

  • Through this agreement, the Nabi Karim (PBUH) was accepted as the head of the state of Madinah, and Madinah was declared the City of Peace, which ended internal revolt and corruption.
  • People of different tribes and religions gathered under one banner, and getting the support of the Jews was a great political achievement.
  • The defence of Madinah became stronger and the foundation of the Islamic state was laid — the Charter was a political and social framework for the first Islamic state.

Key Points

  • Mithaq = treaty; the Charter had 54 articles and was made among Muslims, Jews and other tribes of Madinah.
  • Due to the Charter, Madinah became a city of peace and the Nabi Karim (PBUH) its head of state.

lessons.title: The Battle of Badr (Ghazwa-e-Badr)
lessons.notes_html:
Cause of the Battle

The main cause of the Battle of Badr was that Hazrat Abu Sufyan (who had not yet accepted Islam) was returning from Syria with a big trade caravan of the Makkans — a thousand camels loaded with goods worth about fifty thousand dinars, guarded by only forty men. The economy of Makkah depended on trade, and the trade route to Syria passed near Madinah. Abu Sufyan feared the Muslims might stop the caravan, so he sent a message to Makkah for help, and an army of one thousand men left Makkah to attack the Muslims.

The Battle

  • The battle took place at a place called Badr, which is 80 miles (about 130 kilometres) from Madinah, on 17th Ramadan, 2 A.H. It was the first decisive battle between Islam and disbelief.
  • The Muslims numbered 313 — 84 Muhajireen and 229 Ansar — while the army of the infidels, led by Abu Jahl, consisted of one thousand men.
  • 70 infidels were killed and 70 were taken prisoners, while 14 Muslims were martyred — 6 Muhajireen and 8 Ansar. Among the killed infidels was their leader Abu Jahl, who was killed by two young soldiers, Mu'adh and Mu'awaz (R.A.).

Results of the Battle

  • It was the first decisive battle between truth and falsehood, in which truth won and falsehood failed; the infidels of Makkah faced a humiliating defeat.
  • The pride of the infidels of Makkah was crushed and their downfall began; their great chiefs, including Abu Jahl, were killed.
  • Allah Almighty granted the Muslims victory through unseen divine help by angels, which raised the morale of the Muslims, and after this success Islam began to spread rapidly.

Key Points

  • Badr: 17 Ramadan 2 A.H.; Muslims 313 against 1,000 infidels.
  • The prisoners were not set free without ransom — they were released on ransom or by teaching Muslims.

lessons.title: The Battle of Uhud (Ghazwa-e-Uhud)
lessons.notes_html:
Causes of the Battle

  • In the Battle of Badr, 70 disbelievers of Makkah were killed and 70 made captives, so the Quraysh wanted to take revenge from the Muslims; information about their army was sent to the Nabi Karim (PBUH) by his uncle Hazrat Abbas (R.A.).
  • The tribes sympathetic to the Makkans also provoked them and promised support, and the defeat at Badr had destroyed the honour of the Quraysh, the custodians of the Ka'bah, so they wanted to restore their dignity.

The Battle

  • The battle was fought at the foot of Mount Uhud, about 3 miles from Madinah, on 7th Shawwal, 3 A.H. The army of three thousand infidels was led by Abu Sufyan; it had 200 horses and 3000 camels. The Muslims numbered 700.
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) and the senior Companions were of the opinion to stay inside the city and defend it, but the young Companions advised going out and fighting; seeing their passion for Jihad, the Nabi Karim (PBUH) accepted the advice of the young Companions.
  • He appointed 50 archers at the mountain pass (now known as Jabal Rumaat) under Hazrat Abdullah bin Jubayr Ansari (R.A.) and strictly ordered them not to leave the pass whether the Muslims won or lost. Later, most of the archers left the pass due to a misunderstanding, so Khalid bin Walid attacked from behind and the Muslims suffered a great loss.
  • 70 Muslims were martyred and 22 infidels were killed; the Nabi Karim (PBUH) was also wounded and one of his blessed teeth was broken. Hazrat Hamzah (R.A.) was martyred by a slave named Wahshi.
  • Hazrat Umme Amara (R.A.) fought practically in this battle, defended the Nabi Karim (PBUH) with the sword and received 12 wounds; Hazrat Aisha, Umme Saleet, Umme Aiman and Umme Sulaim (R.A.) kept providing water to the wounded soldiers.

Results

The infidels returned without achieving their objective of eliminating the Muslims, the hypocrites were exposed, and the Muslims learnt the lesson of the importance of obedience.

Key Points

  • Uhud: 7 Shawwal 3 A.H.; Muslims 700 against 3,000 infidels led by Abu Sufyan.
  • The turning point: the archers left the pass of Jabal Rumaat against orders.

lessons.title: The Battle of Trench (Ghazwa-e-Khandaq)
lessons.notes_html:
Meanings of the Names

"Khandaq" (Trench) means a ditch — a long and deep ditch dug for the defence of a city. In this battle the Muslims dug a trench around Madinah, so it is called Ghazwa-e-Khandaq. "Ahzab" means groups or allied parties; many tribes and groups of infidels allied together against the Muslims in this battle, so it is also called Ghazwa-e-Ahzab.

Causes

  • After the defeat of Badr and the indecisive battle of Uhud, the infidels were restless and wanted a decisive war for revenge, so they gathered under the banner of Abu Sufyan.
  • The trade of the Makkans with Syria was under threat, and after the Muslims' control over the trade region of Najd and Iraq, they took extreme measures against the Muslims.

The Battle

  • It was fought at Madinah in Shawwal, 5 A.H. On three sides of Madinah there were mountains, houses and gardens; only the northern side was an open field, so a trench 3.5 miles long, ten yards wide and ten yards deep, was dug on that side.
  • Hazrat Salman Farsi (R.A.) advised to dig the trench, as trenches were dug in Persia (Iran) for the defence of cities. The Nabi Karim (PBUH) adopted the advice and himself took part in the digging; the trench was completed within a week.
  • The combined army of the infidels was ten thousand (four thousand from Makkah alone under Abu Sufyan), while the Muslims were 3000. Madinah was besieged for about a month.
  • The chieftain of Banu Nadhir, Huyayy bin Akhtab, succeeded in convincing the Jews of Banu Qurayzah to break the treaty. During the siege, Hazrat Safiyyah (R.A.) killed a Jew spy and threw his head towards the other Jews.

Results

After about a month's siege, due to a stormy wind and shortage of supplies, the infidels returned unsuccessful; the power of the Quraysh was broken and after this they did not have the courage to attack Madinah.

Key Points

  • Khandaq = trench; Ahzab = the allied parties. Battle fought in Shawwal 5 A.H.
  • Advice to dig the trench: Hazrat Salman Farsi (R.A.); the Prophet (PBUH) dug with his own hands.

lessons.title: Fulfilment of Promise
lessons.notes_html:
What is Keeping a Promise?

The purpose of keeping a promise is that whatever statement, word or oath is made to someone should be fulfilled. Through it, trust is established among people, an atmosphere of truth and honesty is created in society, and a person is known as a good Muslim and a responsible citizen. Whether the promise is made to Allah and His Rasool, to people, or to an organisation, it must be fulfilled in every case. Not coming on time for one's job and neglecting one's duties is also akin to breaking one's promise.

Importance in Islam

  • Allah Almighty has commanded again and again in the Holy Quran to fulfil promises: "O you people who have believed! Fulfil your promises." In the Quran, those who fulfil their promises are declared the successful ones, and Allah Himself never breaks His promise.
  • In Kalimah-e-Tayyibah, we made a promise to Allah and His Rasool (PBUH) that we will follow the commandments of Allah and the Sunnah of the Nabi Karim (PBUH). Allah said: "Fulfil the promise you made to Me; I will fulfil the promise I made to you."
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) said: "He who does not keep his promise has no faith", and he declared breaking a promise a sign of hypocrisy. On the Day of Judgement, a person will also be questioned about his promises.

The Example of the Nabi Karim (PBUH)

  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) was the great person who fulfilled all the promises in his life; he was so famous for keeping promises that even his enemies admitted this virtue. He made agreements with the Jews of Madinah and the infidels of Makkah for the establishment of peace.
  • While leaving for the Battle of Badr, he stopped Hazrat Hudhayfah and his father from joining the battle because of the promise they had made to Abu Jahl, and said: "Fulfil what you have promised; we will pray for help from Allah against them."
  • When Abu Sufyan (who had not yet accepted Islam) appeared in the court of the Roman Emperor Caesar, Caesar asked whether Muhammad (PBUH) kept his promises or not. Abu Sufyan replied: "He does not break promises."

Key Points

  • Keeping promises creates trust, truth and honesty in society.
  • Breaking a promise = a sign of hypocrisy; a promise-keeper has complete faith.

lessons.title: Forgiveness and Forbearance
lessons.notes_html:
Forgiveness

Forgiveness literally means to pardon / to show mercy: to forgive the mistakes and faults of the people and not to take revenge from them for your own sake despite having power and authority to do so. Forgiveness is included in good manners, it is one of the great attributes of Allah, and Islam considers it a sign of a great quality and human dignity.

  • Ayat (Surah An-Nisa: 43): "Indeed, Allah is the Most Pardoning, Often Forgiving."
  • At the conquest of Makkah, the people of Makkah had committed many cruelties against the Nabi Karim (PBUH) and the Muslims, but he granted a general pardon to all of them and did not think of any revenge. Forgiving despite having power is the greatest quality of a human being.

Forbearance

Forbearance means patience: to bear people's ignorance, unnecessary harshness and their offensive words with courage, and not to take personal revenge despite having the power to do so. A forbearing person controls his anger and replies to harsh words in a gentle manner. Bearing someone's unpleasant words is forbearance.

  • At Taif, the people threw stones at the Nabi Karim (PBUH) and he was injured, to the extent that his blessed shoes were filled with blood. The angel of the mountains offered to crush Taif between the two mountains, but he forgave them and said: "I hope that people of faith will be born from their generations."
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) declared that a strong person is the one who controls his anger, not the one who defeats others in wrestling.
  • A person repeatedly asked the Rasool-ul-Allah (PBUH) for advice; he advised him: "Do not be angry."

Benefits

Through forgiveness and forbearance, love and brotherhood increase in society, enmities and quarrels come to an end and peace is established. The person who forgives gains honour in this world and attains the pleasure of Allah and success in the Hereafter. The Nabi Karim's (PBUH) life was a perfect example of forgiveness and forbearance.

Key Points

  • Forgiveness = pardoning despite having power; forbearance = bearing harshness with patience.
  • Best examples: the general pardon at the conquest of Makkah, and the forgiveness of the people of Taif.

lessons.title: Tolerance
lessons.notes_html:
What is Tolerance?

Tolerance means to bear, to endure, to accept and to allow. It means to tolerate the beliefs, opinions and ideas of others against your own with patience, to treat them with kindness, and to give them the right to live according to their own thoughts and beliefs. To force a person to follow a belief other than his own is against tolerance. Islam is a religion of tolerance and forbids forcing anyone in the matter of religion.

  • Ayat (Surah Al-Baqarah: 256): لَا إِكْرَاهَ فِي الدِّينِ — "There is no compulsion in religion." No human being can be forced to become a Muslim or to leave his religion.
  • Ayat (Surah Al-Kafiroon: 6): لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِيَ دِينِ — "To you be your religion and to me my religion."

Examples from the Seerah

  • When a delegation of Christian scholars and leaders from Najran came to meet the Nabi Karim (PBUH), he accommodated them in Masjid-e-Nabawi and treated them with great hospitality. Since it was Sunday, he even allowed them to worship in his own Masjid according to their Christian beliefs — a great example of his tolerance.
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) used to stand up in respect while the funeral of the Jews passed through the streets of Madinah, and he treated the Dhimmis (non-Muslim residents of the Islamic state) with tolerance and kindness.
  • Thumama bin Uthal, who belonged to Yamamah, was so much impressed by the tolerance and good behaviour of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) that he accepted Islam.
  • Muslims ruled the sub-continent for almost a thousand years, but they did not forcibly convert any non-Muslim to Islam.

Rights of Dhimmis

Hazrat Abu Bakr (R.A.) and Hazrat Umar (R.A.) gave the Dhimmis these rights in writing: they will have religious freedom and their places of worship will be protected; no pressure in faith; their forts will not be damaged; their lives and properties will be protected; their disabled and deprived people will be supported from Bait-ul-Mal, and Jizya will not be taken from their poor and deprived ones.

Key Points

  • Tolerance = bearing the beliefs and opinions of others with patience and kindness.
  • Through tolerance, peace, love and brotherhood are established in society.

lessons.title: Mercy
lessons.notes_html:
What is Mercy?

Mercy means treating Allah's creatures with gentleness, love and compassion and practically giving them all kinds of sympathy and help — physically, financially or morally. Allah Almighty is the Most Compassionate and the Most Merciful, and He demands from His servants that they adopt a merciful attitude towards His creation. Mercy gives a man respect in society and brings a person closer to Allah.

  • Ayat: وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِلْعَالَمِينَ — "And (O Prophet!) We have not sent you but as a Mercy for the worlds." (Surah Al-Ambiya: 107) Allah made the Nabi Karim (PBUH) a Mercy for the worlds — not only for Muslims but for every creature of the whole universe.
  • Hadith: "Have mercy on those on earth, the One in heaven (Allah) will have mercy on you." And: "He who does not show mercy to others will not be shown mercy."
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) stated that the one who does not respect elders and does not show kindness to the younger ones is "not from us". He did not take revenge for his own sake.

Examples of the Prophet's Mercy

  • Once a Companion picked up a baby bird, and the mother bird started circling over his head in distress. The Nabi Karim (PBUH) immediately instructed the Companion to put the baby bird back in its nest — he was merciful even towards animals and birds.
  • A man who fetched water for a thirsty dog was given forgiveness by Allah for this kindness.
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) forbade the people to make the animals fight with each other.

Mercy of the Companions

About the mercy of the Companions, Allah Almighty said in Surah Al-Fath (verse 29): "They are kind-hearted and merciful amongst themselves." The wealthy Companions used to help the poor Companions with their wealth and tried to surpass each other in goodness and kindness.

Key Points

  • Kindness does NOT mean to be harsh with Allah's creation — mercy is gentleness and compassion for all creatures.
  • Show mercy to those on earth, and Allah will show mercy to you.

lessons.title: Frugality
lessons.notes_html:
What is Frugality?

Frugality means to spend wealth according to the need while avoiding extravagancy and unnecessary spending. It is the careful management of material resources, especially money. It is a moral quality which makes a person wealthy and peaceful, and saves him from debt and from begging from others. By adopting frugality, a person can spend a life of honour and peace and does not remain needy of anyone.

Miserliness and Extravagance

  • Miserliness is the opposite of frugality: being so stingy that even legitimate needs are not met. A miser does not fulfil even the lawful needs of himself and his family. Miserliness is a bad trait and the root of many evils such as betrayal, dishonesty, cruelty and greed, and Islam dislikes it.
  • Extravagance means wasteful and unnecessary spending of wealth beyond the limit and without need. The extravagant person suffers financial hardship, then adopts illegal means to earn his sustenance and indulges in sinful acts. Allah Almighty does not like the extravagant, and Islam condemns them in the Holy Quran.

Moderation — the Middle Path

  • Hadith: "The best work is that which is based on moderation." Neither miserliness should be practised nor extravagance; Islam praises those who spend with moderation and teaches balance in every matter. A person who adopts moderation does not remain destitute.
  • Ayat (Surah A'raaf: 31): كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا ۚ إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُسْرِفِينَ — "Eat and drink, but do not spend extravagantly, because certainly He does not like the extravagant."
  • Ayat (Surah Al-Furqan: 67): the quality of Allah's special servants is that when they spend, they are neither extravagant nor miserly, and their spending is a balance between the two extremes.

Key Points

  • Frugality ≠ miserliness and ≠ extravagance — it is spending according to need.
  • Example: the frugal friend spends according to his need, saves something, and helps others in difficult times; the extravagant one ends the month asking for loans.

lessons.title: Islamic Brotherhood
lessons.notes_html:
Meaning of Islamic Brotherhood

Islamic brotherhood means that all Muslims, regardless of colour, race, language and country, are brothers of one another. Literally, brotherhood means being brothers, and in Arabic the word "Ukhuwwat" is used for it. This brotherhood is based on faith and makes respect and help of every Muslim obligatory upon another Muslim. Before the advent of the Nabi Karim (PBUH), the people of Arabia were divided into tribes; Islam united them as brothers.

  • Ayat (Surah Al-Hujurat: 10): إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ إِخْوَةٌ — "Indeed, the believers are brothers to one another."
  • Ayat (Surah Al-Tauba: 71): "The believers, men and women, are helpers and friends of one another."
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) established the relationship of brotherhood among the Muhajireen and the Ansar (Muwakhat-e-Madinah) — Islamic brotherhood is not just a verbal claim but the name of practical sacrifice.
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) declared it undesirable for two Muslims to be angry with one another for more than three days.

How Worships Strengthen Brotherhood

  • All Muslims read a single Kalimah and offer the five daily prayers in congregation, standing equal in one row — the rich and the poor together.
  • Through Zakat, the right of the poor comes out of the wealth of the rich and hearts are connected.
  • The fasts of Ramadan give everyone the same experience of hunger and thirst.
  • In Hajj, Muslims from all over the world gather at one place in one dress and practically demonstrate brotherhood.

Benefits of Brotherhood

Islamic brotherhood creates love, compassion, benevolence and self-sacrifice among the Muslims. Due to this relationship, Muslims take part in each other's sufferings and help them, which increases love and makes society strong. Hazrat Umar (R.A.) used to call Hazrat Bilal (R.A.) lessons.title: Manners of Recitation of the Holy Quran
lessons.notes_html:
The Holy Quran

"Quran" means "the book which is read the most" — as this book is read the most of all books, hence it is named the Quran. The Holy Quran is the last divine book of Allah and the source of guidance for all human beings. It was revealed to the Nabi Karim (PBUH), Allah's last Rasool, through Hazrat Jibreel (A.S.), gradually over a period of about 23 years. Allah Almighty has Himself taken the responsibility of guarding the Quran, so despite the passage of more than fourteen hundred years, it is preserved in its original form without any change.

  • Reciting one letter of the Holy Quran yields ten good deeds.
  • The best person is the one who learns the Quran and teaches it to others, and a person who acts upon the instructions of the Holy Quran can attain success in both the worlds.

Manners of Recitation

  • It is very important to be neat, clean and purified (with Wudu) before touching the Quran, and recitation should be done while sitting at a clean and purified place, facing the Qiblah.
  • Before starting the recitation, recite Ta'awwuz and Tasmiyah. Ta'awwuz means reciting "A'uzu billahi minash-shaytanir-rajeem" — seeking Allah's refuge from the accursed Satan. Tasmiyah means reciting "Bismillah-ir-Rahman-ir-Rahim" — beginning in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
  • Recitation should be done slowly and distinctly with serenity and contentment, in a beautiful and pleasant voice, with Tajweed; it is not appropriate to talk during the recitation.
  • Take care of the Rumooz-e-Awqaaf (where to stop and where to continue), and the listeners should listen silently and attentively.

Key Points

  • Before recitation: Wudu, a clean place, Ta'awwuz and Tasmiyah.
  • During recitation: slow, distinct, beautiful voice; no talking; listeners silent.

lessons.title: Hazrat Isa (A.S.)
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction

Hazrat Isa (A.S.) is a beloved servant and Rasool of Allah. His other name mentioned in the Quran and Ahadith is "Messiah" (Al-Masih). He is counted among the Ulul Azm (determined) Prophets of Allah and was sent as a Rasool to the nation of Israel (the Jews). Allah revealed the Injeel upon him, and he was given prophethood at the age of 30.

  • Hazrat Isa (A.S.) was born about five and a half centuries (about 550 years) before the Nabi Karim (PBUH), in the city of Bethlehem in Jerusalem.
  • His mother's name was Hazrat Maryam (A.S.), a pious and pure servant of Allah; her father's name was Imran and her mother's name was Hannah. By His power, Allah gave birth to Hazrat Isa (A.S.) from Hazrat Maryam without a father, and shortly after his birth he started speaking in the lap of his mother.
  • His closest and faithful companions are called "Hawari" (Disciples) — those people of Bani Israel who believed in him and supported him in his preaching. When he was disappointed from the rich people of the Jews, he turned his attention towards the poor and unprivileged people.

The Belief of Muslims about Hazrat Isa (A.S.)

  • Hazrat Isa (A.S.) is the servant and Rasool of Allah; he is neither a god nor a son of God. He used to eat food and drink water and was dependent upon Allah in every action, while Allah is free from every dependency.
  • His extraordinary birth and miracles happened with the permission of Allah.
  • The Jews neither killed him nor crucified him; rather, Allah raised him to the heavens alive with respect. He is alive in the heavens and, before the Day of Resurrection, Allah will send him to earth again and Dajjal will be killed by him.

Key Points

  • Other name: Al-Masih; mother: Hazrat Maryam (A.S.); book: Injeel; companions: Hawari.
  • Muslims believe he was raised alive to the heavens and will return before the Day of Resurrection.

lessons.title: Hazrat Usman Ghani (R.A.)
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction

Hazrat Usman (R.A.) belonged to the famous Banu Umayyah branch of the Quraysh, and his lineage is traced to the Nabi Karim's (PBUH) ancestors in the fifth generation. His father's name was Affan and his mother was Arwa; his Kunya was Abu Abdullah and Abu Umar. For the sake of Islam, he endured the persecution of the infidels and took part in two migrations (to Abyssinia and to Madinah).

  • His title was "Zun-Noorain" — "the one who has two lights" — because the Nabi Karim (PBUH) married his two daughters, Sayyida Ruqayyah and Sayyida Umme Kulthum (R.A.), one after the other, to Hazrat Usman (R.A.).
  • Due to his wealth and generosity, he was also called "Ghani" (the Rich one).

Services for Islam

  • At the time of shortage of fresh water in Madinah, he bought the well Beir Rumah from a Jew — half for 12,000 dirhams and the other half for 8,000 dirhams (20,000 dirhams in all) — and dedicated the whole well for the use of the Muslims.
  • On the occasion of the Battle of Tabuk, he bore a great share of the expenses of the army and offered 1,000 camels, 70 horses and 1,000 dinars in cash. Seeing this, the Nabi Karim (PBUH) said: "After today, no action of Usman can harm him."
  • First of all, Hazrat Abdul Rahman bin Awf (R.A.) pledged allegiance to Hazrat Usman (R.A.) as Caliph, and after the pledge of Hazrat Ali (R.A.), all other people also made pledge of allegiance to him.

Caliphate and Martyrdom

  • His caliphate lasted from 24 A.H. to 35 A.H. — a few days short of twelve years. During his caliphate the Islamic state expanded, and the first six years passed with widespread peace and great victories.
  • He was martyred on Friday, 18 Dhu Al-Hajj, 35 A.H. A rebellious group from Egypt attacked his house; at that time he was reciting the Holy Quran. He was 82 years old at the time of martyrdom.

Key Points

  • Titles: Zun-Noorain and Ghani; branch: Banu Umayyah of Quraysh.
  • Famous services: buying Beir Rumah for the Muslims and the great spending at Tabuk.

lessons.title: Hazrat Khalid bin Walid (R.A.)
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction

Hazrat Khalid bin Walid (R.A.) belonged to the famous Banu Makhzum branch of the Quraysh. His Kunya (surname) was Abu Sulaiman, and his mother Asma bint Haris was the sister of Umm-ul-Momineen Hazrat Maimunah (R.A.). He accepted Islam in 8 A.H. and became one of the bravest and most famous generals of Islam; his whole life was spent doing Jihad for Islam, and he never faced defeat in any battle.

The Battle of Moota and the Title Saifullah

  • In the Battle of Moota, three thousand Muslims faced one hundred thousand Roman (Christian) soldiers. When all three appointed commanders were martyred one after the other, Hazrat Khalid bin Walid (R.A.) took up the flag.
  • He fought with such bravery that nine of his swords were broken while fighting, and finally one Yemeni sword was left in his hand. With his wisdom and bravery, he brought the remaining Muslim army out of the grip of the enemies safely.
  • Upon this, the Nabi Karim (PBUH) awarded him the title of "Saifullah" — "the Sword of Allah" — saying that one of the swords of Allah took the flag in his hand and Allah blessed his hands with victory.

Later Services

  • During the caliphate of Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (R.A.), he was sent for suppressing those who denied to pay Zakat and the apostates, and under his command the Muslim army wiped them out.
  • Hazrat Umar (R.A.) removed him from the commandership of Syria.
  • This great hero of Islam died in 21 A.H. in Syria.

Key Points

  • Branch: Banu Makhzum; Kunya: Abu Sulaiman; title: Saifullah (the Sword of Allah).
  • At Moota: 3,000 Muslims against 100,000 Romans; nine swords broken; army saved.
